items.title: AuChau
items.description: Learning-management platform for a multi-branch English center — staff run the centre from a web portal, while students and parents get their own schedule, scores and tuition on their phones.
items.overview: The system a multi-branch English centre runs on: staff handle classes, schedules, scoring and tuition from a web portal, while students and parents see the same information on a mobile app. I built the **mobile half** — the app and the API behind it — then automated two jobs the office did by hand: **end-of-term class rollover** and **the monthly reports**.
items.businessContext: Staff had a web system; **families were locked out of it**. Any question about class times, scores or tuition meant phoning the office. The goal was to hand that straight to families without forking the business logic — **one backend, a second client**.
items.roleSummary: **Backend & Mobile Developer** on a **six-person team** across three repos. The Vue staff portal was built by others.
responsibilities: **Mobile API** — **11 controllers** over schedules, attendance, exams, scores, tuition, homework and leave
**Student and parent screens** in the React Native app
**Push pipeline**: FCM plus a dispatcher fanning one event to the student and every linked parent
**Nightly class rollover** with room allocation and holiday handling
**Classroom scheduling** with room and time-slot conflict validation
**Academic and revenue reports**, exported to the centre's Excel templates
features: 🗓️ **Schedule**: next session with teacher, room and slot, plus the week ahead and exam dates.
✅ **Attendance**: present, absent or excused, per session.
📊 **Scores**: by class and assessment component, not one average.
💵 **Tuition**: what is owed and what is paid, per child.
📚 **Homework**: assignments, deadlines, file upload, teacher attachments.
🧾 **Leave requests**: parents file, edit and withdraw them themselves.
🎬 **Courses**: class overview, weekly progress, video lessons.
🔔 **Alerts**: push on schedule changes, absences, leave decisions, tuition and exams.
👨‍👩‍👧 **Family accounts**: a parent switches between children; each sees only their own.
📤 **Staff reporting**: one-click Excel into the office's existing workbooks.
highlights: **Ownership guard** read from the token — a request carrying someone else's studentId is refused
One dispatcher behind **ten event types**, **fire-and-forget** so a failed push never breaks the request
Nightly rollover allocates rooms around clashes, skips holidays, and is **idempotent** against manual creation
Mobile API **released separately** from the staff API, so app builds never wait on the portal
Excel export writes **only the input columns** and lets the workbook's own formulas do the rest
impact: **Live in production** — students, parents and staff use it daily
Routine questions **answered in-app** instead of by phone
End-of-term class creation went from **manual, per class** to a **nightly job**
Monthly reports **export straight from the system**

challenges.title: End-of-term class rollover was manual
challenges.problem: Staff hand-created the next class for every group — free room, re-enrol students, lay sessions and exams around holidays. **Dozens of times a term**, and a missed clash surfaced only when students met an occupied room.
challenges.solution: A **nightly job** picks up classes ending within 14 days, finds a free room per slot, generates sessions and exams (cancelling holidays), migrates active students and notifies families. **Idempotent**: it skips if a next-level class already holds them.
challenges.result: Rollover happens **overnight**, and manual and automatic creation **coexist safely**.

challenges.title: Five modules all needed to notify families
challenges.problem: Scores, schedules, attendance, tuition and exams each had to reach families. Wiring Firebase into all five **scatters the same fan-out logic**, and a stale device token would fail the request behind it — saving a score should not depend on a push.
challenges.solution: **One dispatcher**, a method per event. Each call opens its own DI scope and runs **fire-and-forget**: persist first, then push. Missing Firebase credentials degrade to database-only.
challenges.result: **Ten event types share one path**; a push outage degrades the notification, not the operation.

items.title: Tapo
items.description: A B2C laptop store built end to end — catalog and checkout for customers, order, inventory and chat desks for staff — as a place to practise production patterns rather than tutorial ones.
items.overview: A single-store B2C platform for laptop retail, **built solo front to back**: Spring Boot behind Nginx in Docker, a React SPA, Supabase PostgreSQL and Upstash Redis. It covers **the whole retail loop** across four RBAC roles, backed by **205 backend and 25 frontend tests**.
items.businessContext: I wanted a project whose hard parts were **a real shop's, not a CRUD tutorial's**: money that must not be charged twice, stock that must not oversell in a flash sale, a token refresh that survives concurrent requests. Retail was the domain because all of those fall out of it naturally.
items.roleSummary: **Sole developer** — domain, backend, front end, tests and the containerised deployment.
responsibilities: **Domain and PostgreSQL schema** — **26 entities**, versioned with Flyway
**Spring Boot API**: 23 controllers, service layer, global exception handling
**Auth**: JWT with Redis-backed refresh tokens, Google OAuth2, email verification, **four-role RBAC**
**React SPA**: storefront, cart, checkout, plus a separate admin area
**Integrations**: PayOS, Supabase Storage and Gmail SMTP
**205 backend tests** (controller, service, H2 flows) and **25 frontend tests**
**Deployment**: Docker Compose behind Nginx, SPA on Vercel
features: 🛍️ **Browse and buy**: search and filters, a cart that survives login, checkout through PayOS.
📦 **Order tracking**: full lifecycle from PENDING to DELIVERED.
⭐ **Reviews and returns**: star reviews held for approval, return requests customers can follow.
🏷️ **Vouchers and flash sales**: usage-capped discounts, stock-limited sales on a countdown.
💬 **Live chat**: customers reach sales staff over WebSocket without leaving the page.
🔐 **Ways in**: email with verification or Google — four staff roles, each landing somewhere different.
📦 **Warehouse desk**: stock import/export, auto-deduction on delivery, low-stock alerts.
📊 **Admin dashboard**: revenue charts, order stats, blog, banners, users.
💳 **Instalments**: a 6 / 12 / 18 / 24-month calculator on the product page.
🌐 **Bilingual**: Vietnamese and English throughout.
highlights: Refresh tokens in **Redis, not the database** — rotation and revocation are one key operation
The SPA **queues every concurrent 401 behind a single refresh** instead of firing one per request
Rate limiting with Bucket4j over Redis, so the limit **holds across instances** rather than per process
A **reflection test asserts every endpoint carries its RBAC annotation** — it catches the route someone forgot to guard
**205 backend tests at three levels**: MockMvc controllers, service units, and H2 integration flows
impact: **Feature-complete retail loop** — catalog, cart, payment, reviews, returns, vouchers, flash sales, inventory
**205 backend and 25 frontend tests passing**, including flows against an in-memory database
**Two security holes** found and closed in a self-review pass, both now covered by tests
Packaged for deployment: SPA on Vercel, backend **containerised behind Nginx**

challenges.title: Concurrent requests hitting a just-expired token
challenges.problem: The SPA fires several calls at once, so they 401 together and a naive interceptor sends **one refresh per call**. The second arrives with a token the first already rotated away, **logging the user out mid-session** — intermittently, so it read as a flaky backend.
challenges.solution: **Queued it**: the first 401 starts one refresh promise, the rest subscribe and replay once it resolves. Tokens sit in Redis so rotation is a single key operation, and the queue is pinned by unit tests.
challenges.result: Token expiry became **invisible**, and a stale refresh no longer cascades into a forced logout.

challenges.title: Blog formatting that also allowed script injection
challenges.problem: Post content rendered through **dangerouslySetInnerHTML** so authors could use bold markers — so any script in a post body ran in the reader's browser. **The feature and the hole were one line of code.**
challenges.solution: Replaced it with a **renderBold()** that parses only the bold marker and returns React nodes, **escaping the rest as text**. Exported so it could be unit-tested against script payloads.
challenges.result: Formatting kept, **injection closed**, and tests fail if raw HTML is reintroduced.

items.title: Trava
items.description: Multi-workspace task and team-collaboration system — private and team spaces, nested tasks, invitations and notifications, built to work through Clean Architecture and CQRS on a domain complex enough to justify them.
items.overview: A task and collaboration system: work lives in **private or team Spaces**, splits into parent and sub-tasks with priorities and workload points, and pushes notifications on assignment and deadlines. Built solo — domain, backend and Angular client — as the project where I would **actually apply Clean Architecture and CQRS** rather than read about them.
items.businessContext: Every task tool I had used drew its boundaries differently and I wanted to know why — **where a workspace ends and a project begins**, how permissions differ between a space you own and one you were invited to. **Collaboration forces those decisions**; a single-user todo list never has to answer them.
items.roleSummary: **Sole developer** — domain, backend architecture, API and the Angular client.
responsibilities: **Domain model**: Spaces and membership roles, nested tasks, priorities and workload points
**Five Clean Architecture projects** with a strictly one-way dependency flow
**CQRS with MediatR**, FluentValidation on commands, AutoMapper between entities and DTOs
**Persistence** on EF Core and PostgreSQL behind Repository and Unit of Work
**Redis distributed caching**, JWT auth, rate limiting and CORS
**Angular client** with PrimeNG and Tailwind
features: 🏢 **Workspaces**: private spaces for your own work, team spaces with role-based access.
📩 **Invitations**: send and accept invites, with invitation state tracked throughout.
✅ **Nested tasks**: sub-tasks, priority from low to urgent, workload points.
💬 **Comments**: discussion attached to the task it concerns.
🔔 **Notifications**: space changes, task assignment, approaching deadlines.
👤 **Accounts**: registration, login, profile and security settings.
highlights: **Five-project Clean Architecture** with a one-way dependency flow — Domain depends on nothing, **persistence never leaks upward**
CQRS through MediatR, with FluentValidation as a pipeline step so **validation sits outside the handler**
Repository and Unit of Work over EF Core, so a request touching several aggregates **still commits once**
**Redis distributed caching** over the read-heavy queries, plus rate limiting on the API surface
JWT with **per-space role checks** — membership of one workspace grants nothing in another
impact: A working collaboration backend covering **the full loop**: space → invite → task → sub-task → comment → notification
Adding a feature means **adding a handler, not editing a controller** — which was the point of the exercise

items.title: PhyGen
items.description: Exam generator for physics teachers — declare the spread of chapters and difficulty you want, and the system assembles a matching paper from a curated question bank.
items.overview: So physics teachers **stop assembling exams by hand**. A teacher defines an **exam matrix** — how many questions, from which chapter, at which difficulty — and the system draws from a curated bank to produce a matching paper, exportable to Word or PDF. I worked on the backend and **owned the repository**, reviewing and merging the team's work. Our graduation capstone.
items.businessContext: Building a physics exam is repetitive without being mechanical: a teacher must **hit a required spread across chapters and difficulty** while keeping papers different between classes, so in practice they reuse last year's or spend an evening on it. An explicit matrix **hands the tedious half to the computer**.
items.roleSummary: **Backend Developer** on a capstone team, and **owner of the backend repository** — reviewing and merging the team's pull requests and managing release branches.
responsibilities: **Backend modules** on a five-project .NET 8 Clean Architecture solution over PostgreSQL
**Curriculum hierarchy** — Curriculum → Subject → Chapter → Topic → Section
**Question bank** and the matrix-driven exam generation flow
**Auth**: registration and login with email OTP, plus role-based access to the shared bank
**Integrations**: Cloudinary for question media, PayOS for payments
**Code review** — merged the team's backend pull requests
features: 🏫 **Curriculum**: Curriculum → Subject → Chapter → Topic → Section, so questions attach where they belong.
📝 **Question bank**: several question types, media per question, categorised by chapter and difficulty.
⚙️ **Matrix generation**: declare the spread you want and the system assembles a matching paper.
📄 **Export**: exams out to Word or PDF, ready to print.
🔐 **Accounts**: email OTP on registration and login, roles over who edits the shared bank.
💳 **Payments**: PayOS checkout for paid plans.
🔔 **Notifications**: course, exam and transaction status.
💬 **Support**: an in-app chatbox for user questions.
highlights: The exam matrix is a **first-class entity, not a filter** — a paper is produced by satisfying a declared spread, which makes the output **reproducible**
Clean Architecture across five projects, keeping **generation logic in the domain** instead of in controllers
**Email OTP** on registration and login, with **RBAC** over who may edit the shared question bank
Cloudinary for question media so **images live outside the database**, PayOS for payment
**Redis caching** over the curriculum and question reads the generator hits repeatedly
impact: Turned exam assembly from **an evening of manual work** into **declaring a matrix and exporting the result**
Delivered as the team's **graduation capstone project**
Packaged with **Docker Compose** so the API and its dependencies come up together

items.title: TimeSwap
items.description: Time-exchange marketplace where people trade hours of skill — post a job, apply with your profile, and settle through an in-app wallet.
items.overview: Connects people with spare time to people who need help, mostly in services and IT. Users post jobs, search by industry, fee and location, apply with their existing profile, and employers review applicants before picking one; payment settles through an **in-app wallet**. Built by a student team across **an Angular web app, a Kotlin Android app and the shared .NET API** behind both.
items.businessContext: Small tasks — an hour of tutoring, an afternoon fixing a laptop — are **too small for a formal freelance platform and too awkward for a group chat**. TimeSwap frames them as **time exchanged rather than a contract signed**: a job carries a fee, anyone applies with the profile they have, and the wallet settles it.
items.roleSummary: **Backend Developer** on a student team, on the **.NET API serving both** the Angular web client and the Kotlin Android app.
responsibilities: **API endpoints** on the .NET 8 backend over PostgreSQL
**Job posting, search and application flow**, including the employer's applicant list
**JWT authentication** serving both the web and Android clients
**E-wallet** and transaction history module
**ChatGPT API** behind the in-app assistant
features: 👤 **Accounts**: registration and login, password reset, profile management.
📋 **Job board**: browse what is open, or search by name, fee, industry, category and location.
📝 **Post and apply**: post a job with its fee; apply with the profile you already have.
🧑‍💼 **Applicant review**: an employer sees everyone who applied and picks the candidate.
💳 **E-wallet**: pay and get paid in-app, with transaction history.
🤖 **Assistant**: a ChatGPT-backed chatbot for job-related questions.
📱 **Android client**: the same marketplace as a native app.
highlights: **One API serving two very different clients** — an Angular SPA and a native Android app — behind a single JWT scheme
Job search across name, fee, industry, category and location through **one query surface**, not an endpoint per filter
E-wallet with transaction history, so a job's fee **settles inside the platform** instead of out of band
**ChatGPT** integrated as an in-app assistant for job-related questions
**Split deployment with CI**: Angular on Vercel, .NET API on DigitalOcean behind Nginx, built by GitHub Actions
impact: **Live and reachable** — the web client runs at swap-time.vercel.app
Delivered across **three surfaces from one backend**: Angular web, Kotlin Android, and the shared .NET API

items.title: Adobe Migration
items.description: Consolidating thousands of a global brand's landing pages off legacy CMS platforms onto Adobe Experience Manager — live customer-facing pages, so the acceptance bar was fidelity, not just a successful import.
items.overview: A global enterprise client was moving its landing pages off several legacy CMS platforms onto **Adobe Experience Manager**. I migrated and validated those pages — **thousands of them** — making sure structure and content **survived intact** across the client's regional environments, inside a strictly governed Agile process.
items.businessContext: The client's landing pages had accumulated across several legacy CMS platforms, each with its own structure, turning every global campaign into **a per-platform exercise**. Consolidating onto AEM gave marketing **one place to author** — but only if migrated pages matched the originals, since these were **live pages for a global brand**.
items.roleSummary: **Software Engineer** on the migration team — migrating and validating landing pages, and holding content consistent across regional environments.
responsibilities: **Migrated** landing pages from legacy CMS platforms onto Adobe Experience Manager
**Validated** each page against its original for structural and content fidelity
**Held content consistent** across global environments, not one region at a time
**Governed Agile process** — work tracked and reviewed through Jira
features: 📄 **Thousands of landing pages** moved off legacy platforms onto a single AEM instance.
✅ **Every page checked against its original** — fidelity, not just a successful import.
🌍 **The same component renders identically** in every regional environment.
🔄 Delivered through a **strictly governed enterprise Agile workflow**.
highlights: The acceptance bar was **fidelity, not import success** — a page that loaded but shifted structure was a defect, which makes **validation the real work**
**Content consistency held across regional AEM environments**, where a component had to behave the same everywhere
Delivered under **enterprise change governance**: batches tracked, reviewed and signed off before reaching a live environment
impact: **Thousands of landing pages** consolidated from several legacy CMS platforms onto **one AEM platform**
**Sixteen months** inside an enterprise delivery process — governed releases, global environments, live customer-facing pages
